item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to minimize. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. This framing gets the opportunity backwards. AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team that competes against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to state clearly that people interact with AI. It also requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content, including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026. Following the 2026 Digital Omnibus, generative AI systems already on the market before that date get an extended transitional period to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.

It documents it.

You may build or operate a recommender system in the EU. It could be a “you might also like” feature, a personalized feed, or a ranking algorithm. This admission from the regulator matters more than any single law firm’s reading of the rules.

item.title: Claude Usage Limits 2026: The Complete Guide
item.description:
Last reviewed and updated on 8 September 2026 against Anthropic’s official documentation.

Claude’s usage limits are one of the most-asked, least-clearly-answered questions for daily work use. Help articles, forum threads, and blog posts scatter the mechanics, plan differences, and cost tradeoffs. This guide puts the complete picture in one place: mechanics, plans, cost, and a decision framework.

How Claude’s usage limits actually work

Claude’s usage limit is not a daily message cap. It does not reset at midnight. It runs on a rolling 5-hour window that starts from the moment you send your first message. If you send your first message at 09:47, your window runs until 14:47. It does not run to the top of the next hour or to a fixed daily timestamp.

item.title: The AI Act Omnibus Delay: Relief or a Trap for Small Teams?
item.description: The headline version of the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI is simple. The EU pushed the high-risk rules back. Stand-alone high-risk systems now have until 2 December 2027. High-risk systems embedded in regulated products have until 2 August 2028. Both dates are later than the original 2 August 2026 date. This headline will cost some small teams a compliance scramble in eighteen months. They will read “delayed” as “cancelled” and stop preparing.

item.title: GPAI Code of Practice: Provider vs. Deployer, Explained
item.description: Does the GPAI Code of Practice apply to you? For most teams that build AI-powered products, the answer is no. The Code is the European Commission’s voluntary compliance tool for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act. The Commission published it on 10 July 2025 after input from more than 1,000 stakeholders. It binds model providers, not the teams that build on top of their models. This guide walks through the provider-vs-deployer test, what each of the Code’s three chapters covers, and what a downstream team building on GPT, Claude, or similar models should take from it.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 25: When You Become the AI 'Provider'
item.description:
Most agencies I speak to treat the EU AI Act as someone else’s problem. They use AI tools, so they assume the heavy obligations sit upstream with OpenAI, Anthropic, or whichever vendor built the model. Almost none of them have read Article 25. This clause moves the provider’s entire obligation set onto ordinary businesses through work they do every week.

This is the most overlooked liability transfer in the Act for creative, marketing, consulting, and research agencies. It does not require you to build a model. It requires you to put a logo on something, adjust it, or point it at a new job. These are the exact activities agencies are paid for.

item.title: EU AI Act AI System Definition: The Official 7-Element Test
item.description: The EU AI Act only applies to systems that meet the legal definition of an “AI system” in Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. This guide explains the European Commission’s official 7-element test. Difference between Communication and Dissemination
item.description:

Communication and dissemination aren’t the same thing — and treating them separately is what makes your research stand out.

Communication builds your credibility over time. It’s broad and ongoing — papers, conference talks, the general visibility you build just by doing good research and showing up in your field.

Dissemination works differently. It’s the deliberate, targeted transfer of your research to specific audiences who can use it — think podcasts, videos, webinars, press releases.

item.description:
In this episode

  • How Mete’s group studies light and matter one photon and one electron spin at a time, to build quantum networks and quantum sensors
  • How a quantum dot can entangle a photon with an electron spin, and why quantum repeaters, not amplifiers, are needed to carry that entanglement over long distances
  • Why no single material does it all: quantum dots for photons, diamond for long-lived spins, and hexagonal boron nitride that works at almost any temperature
  • How nanodiamond sensors inside living cells and worms can report temperature, magnetic fields and pH from the inside
  • His path from Bilkent University in Turkey via Boston and ETH Zurich to Cambridge, and the result he picked: showing that a single photon’s electric field can be quieter than vacuum
  • His three wishes: keep working with great teams, find unallocated time to think, and steady baseline funding

Key Takeaways

  • Professor at University of Cambridge studying light–matter interaction at the quantum level in semiconductors, diamond and 2D materials, for quantum networks and quantum sensors.
  • Adding the electron spin to the single photon opens a new dimension: photon–spin entanglement lets you distribute entanglement between distant nodes and use quantum dots as quantum repeaters (no amplifiers, per no-cloning).
  • No single material wins: quantum dots are the best single-photon source, diamond the best spin/memory, hBN is temperature-agnostic (good for space).
  • Nanodiamond NV-centre sensors can go inside living cells (even C. elegans) to non-destructively map magnetic field, pH, temperature and viscosity at the nanoscale, a surprise life-sciences application.
  • Career: Turkey → Boston → ETH Zurich → Cambridge; champions researcher mobility. Wishes: keep the same calibre of team, unallocated thinking time, and steady baseline funding.

About the guest

Mete Atature is a Professor at the University of Cambridge in the UK, whose research explores the interaction of light and matter at the quantum level, including quantum sensing networks and secure communication.

item.description:
In this episode

  • What “hot” single photons are: light emitted at room temperature, and why photons from samples cooled close to absolute zero are cleaner
  • Why defects in hexagonal boron nitride can emit single photons without a cryostat, and how Carlos’s team creates them
  • A European project to send room-temperature single photons 700 metres through the air for secure communication
  • His path from Madrid, via Pascale Senellart’s group in Paris and 2D materials in Würzburg and Oldenburg, back to a tenure track at the Autonomous University of Madrid
  • The experiment he is proudest of: two quick laser pulses that made a quantum dot emit an entangled state of photons and vacuum, with a surprising link to the Fibonacci sequence
  • His wishes: less bureaucracy, unlimited funding and a good coffee machine for the lab

Key Takeaways

  • Tenure-track researcher at the Autonomous University of Madrid working on ‘hot’ (room-temperature) single photons from defects in hexagonal boron nitride, alongside continued work on semiconductor quantum dots.
  • Cold vs hot single photons: cooling quiets crystal vibrations to give identical, interference-ready photons; room-temperature photons carry more noise but need no cryostat, so they suit drones, cars, satellites.
  • hBN is currently the front-runner room-temperature single-photon material; defects can be placed deterministically by electron irradiation of flakes.
  • Advice he passes on: change material platform (a calculated risk) between PhD and postdoc, and build broad international experience and networks before setting up a group.
  • Leads a QuantERA project (COMPHORT, with Tobias Heindel) targeting 700 m free-space quantum key distribution with hot single photons by 2027; wishes for less bureaucracy, more funding, and a good coffee machine.

About the guest

Carlos Antós Solanas is a Professor at the Autonomous University of Madrid in Spain, where he researches hot single photons for quantum communication, especially in hexagonal boron nitride at room temperature. After his PhD in Madrid, he was a postdoc in Pascale Senellart’s group, supported by a Marie Curie fellowship (2015 to 2019), then worked on 2D materials with Christian Schneider in Würzburg and Oldenburg (2020 to 2022), before returning to Madrid through the Atracción de Talento programme.

Key Takeaways

  • Deputy director of the BELLA Center at Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, shrinking kilometre-scale particle accelerators to centimetres using high-intensity lasers and plasmas, 1 GeV in ~3 cm vs ~100–300 m conventionally.
  • Compact/mobile accelerators could enable field science, truck-mounted or endoscopic cancer therapy for less wealthy countries, smaller free-electron lasers, and affordable next-generation TeV colliders.
  • Machine learning is central for stabilising and optimising these compact accelerators; ~50 groups worldwide work on plasma acceleration, with Berkeley among the strongest.
  • Academia–industry partnership works because national labs provide the expensive infrastructure and companies provide product focus.
  • Three wishes: ‘money, time and wisdom’, more time (esp. work/family balance), more funding, and the foresight to pick the right, realistic projects.

item.title: Nanoscience revolusionizing Green Chemistry?
Nanoscience revolusionizing Green Chemistry?
Nanoscience revolusionizing Green Chemistry? ft. Julio Terra
item.description:
In this episode

  • What green chemistry means, and why small changes to a catalyst can make a whole chemical process greener
  • Why the pharmaceutical industry produces around 90% waste for 10% product, and how Julio made a rose fragrance and amines in fewer steps
  • What heterogeneous catalysis is, explained with salt and sand in water
  • His path from an agricultural university near his village in Brazil, via Toronto and McGill, to a postdoc at EPFL
  • How trapping reactions inside tiny pores changes the chemistry, explained with The Little Prince, and how this kept hydrogen in place long enough to use it
  • His three wishes for science: more LGBTQ people, more women and more BIPOC people

Key Takeaways

  • Catalysis sits in almost every chemical product, so small tweaks to a catalyst change a whole process, less energy, higher selectivity, less waste; this is the lever green chemistry pulls.
  • Pharma is the worst offender (~90% waste, 10% product) because molecules need many low-yield steps, and most of that waste is solvent, which chemists routinely ignore.
  • Concrete wins: making rose-oxide fragrance (multi-ton scale) via a photochemical step (light is abundant and safer than heat), and making amines in one step that reincorporates fragments that would otherwise be waste (atom economy).
  • Heterogeneous catalysis (sand-in-water, not salt-in-water) lets you filter or settle out scarce, toxic metal catalysts so they don’t end up in the product.
  • Confinement effect: molecules in spaces near their own size constantly hit the walls and each other and so react differently, he trapped in-situ-generated hydrogen in tiny nanospheres so it’s consumed before it escapes, and wrote a COVID-lockdown review on using confinement to make chemistry greener.
  • The green-chemistry community is unusually tight-knit and welcoming, and courses/summer schools now exist where they didn’t in his undergrad; he came to chemistry wanting to teach and values science’s global, people-centred side. Three wishes: more LGBTQ, women and BIPOC people in STEM.
Listen on

About the guest

Julio Terra is a Post-doctoral Associate at EPFL in Switzerland, where he designs nanostructures with controlled composition, size and shape to make catalysts for green chemistry. In his PhD at McGill University, he trapped a catalyst inside hollow silica shells to study confined chemistry. He obtained his BSc and MSc in Chemistry in Brazil, with exchanges at the University of Toronto and McGill.

Perfect Broccoli & Quantum Thermometers ft. George Mihailescu
item.description:
In this episode

  • How George moved from a physics with biomedical sciences degree to a PhD in quantum technologies at University College Dublin
  • What a quantum battery is, and why one won’t be in your phone any time soon
  • Why an Irish startup wants to build quantum computers on CMOS, the chip technology already inside phones and laptops
  • How quantum computing could speed up training AI models such as ChatGPT
  • His first PhD project: using a quantum system as a thermometer for quantum samples such as graphene and metals, and why precise temperatures matter for quantum devices
  • His three wishes: more time, PhD stipends you can live on in Ireland, and a better laptop keyboard

Key Takeaways

  • A quantum system used as a temperature probe gives the most precise measurement physically possible, which matters because quantum devices only work in a narrow temperature window and thermal fluctuations destroy the quantum states they rely on.
  • His first PhD result: this quantum thermometry gives a robust, well-defined response across very different samples (graphene, twisted bilayer graphene, metals), even though correlations and entanglement build up between probe and sample.
  • Equal1’s bet: CMOS is cheap, ubiquitous and scalable, so even if its qubits are noisier and more error-prone than other platforms, having far more of them (and possibly running warmer) could compensate.
  • Quantum batteries store energy in a quantum system’s energy levels/coherences; the models map to real systems but it’s unclear any exist in a lab, and heat or a drop would spoil the state, so not in your phone.
  • Link to AI: a quantum speed-up in accessing huge datasets or training models could make better models arrive sooner. Space wouldn’t obviously help, fewer thermal fluctuations but other radiation, and a lab is more controllable.
  • On the profession: Irish PhD stipends fall below cost of living although PhDs work more than 9-to-5, carry teaching load off professors, and raise the university’s status.
Listen on

About the guest

George Mihailescu is a PhD Researcher at University College Dublin in Ireland, studying miniaturised technologies and how to control them for sensing and computation. His first PhD project uses an impurity or qubit as a thermometer for quantum environments, where temperature fluctuations can destroy fragile quantum states. He holds a Bachelor’s in Physics and Biomedical Sciences and a Master’s in Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics from UCD.

She studied at the University of Kansas, did her PhD at Caltech and a postdoc at Stanford, where she joined the faculty before moving to Florida. Her research group develops precursor compounds for making thin films and nanostructures. She has since been elected president-elect of the American Chemical Society, serving as president in 2028.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence meets Nanoscience with Andy Sode Anker
item.description:
Andy Sode Anker’s group makes new functional materials, takes them to synchrotrons to follow the chemistry with X-rays as it happens, and ends up with a lot of data. Analysing that data with artificial intelligence is, in his words, the core of his research. He moved from the lab bench to data after deciding he was too clumsy and not patient enough for lab work.

About the guest

Andy Sode Anker was a PhD student in materials chemistry at the University of Copenhagen when we recorded this episode in late 2022. He grew up on the Danish island of Bornholm and worked closely with the university’s Department of Computer Science. He has since moved to the Technical University of Denmark, where he continues to develop machine learning methods for analysing X-ray scattering data from nanomaterials.

item.title: Graphene Nanotunnels: Welcome Onboard with Ashok Keerthi
item.description:
Manchester is known for making graphene by peeling one layer off a graphite crystal. Ashok Keerthi does the opposite: he removes a layer from the middle of a stack of 2D crystals, leaving tunnels only atoms high, and studies how molecules move through them. In one test, helium came out about a hundred times faster than expected.

About the guest

Ashok Keerthi is a chemist in the Department of Chemistry at the University of Manchester, where he held a Presidential Fellowship at the time of this 2022 recording, a research-focused route equivalent to assistant professor. He studied up to his master’s in India, did a PhD in synthetic organic chemistry at the National University of Singapore, and was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Germany. His group studies molecular transport through capillaries made with atomic-scale precision and also makes graphene nanoribbons from the bottom up.

item.title: Shattering a 10000-Year-Old Ceramic Recipe
item.description:
Claire Dancer says ceramics get overlooked because people think they are brittle, yet we use them all the time, from mugs and plates to light fittings and plug sockets. Making them traditionally means firing a powder in a furnace well above 1,000 °C for a long time. Her group works on new ways to make ceramics at much lower temperatures and with far less energy.

About the guest

Claire Dancer is a Reader at WMG, University of Warwick, in the UK, where she has led a ceramic processing group since 2013. She grew up near Cardiff, studied natural sciences and materials science at Cambridge, and did her PhD at Oxford on magnesium diboride, a superconductor. Postdocs on ceramic armour and on metamaterials followed. According to her Warwick profile, she also leads outreach and engagement for the UK Metamaterials Network.

His group makes them in about an hour instead of days, and he studies whether they hold up at high temperatures. He also learned, after a swim in a cold Lake Zurich, that thermodynamics always wins.

About the guest

Jose Luis Ocaña-Pujol was a PhD student at ETH Zurich in Switzerland when we recorded this episode in 2022. He studied nanoscience at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, then took a master’s in Science for Energy and Sustainability in Amsterdam, which included research at AMOLF and a part-time job in energy analysis. His 2022 paper with colleagues at ETH Zurich, Strain-Driven Thermal and Optical Instability in Silver/Amorphous-Silicon Hyperbolic Metamaterials, was published in Advanced Optical Materials.

About the guest

Rebecca Pittkowski was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Copenhagen when we recorded this episode in 2022. She now leads the Nanoparticles in Electrocatalysis group as an assistant professor in the Department of Chemistry at the University of Copenhagen. Her group makes metal and oxide nanoparticles for water electrolysis and fuel cells, and studies them with synchrotron X-ray techniques.

item.description:
Julien Barrier works in mesoscopic transport, a branch of physics at the intersection of quantum mechanics and classical physics. He builds graphene devices, cools them to tens of millikelvin, and measures their electrical properties, looking for phenomena that can’t be found in larger or smaller devices. He does it in Manchester, where graphene was discovered.

About the guest

Julien Barrier is an experimental physicist who trained in chemical physics at ESPCI Paris and did his master’s project at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. He moved to the University of Manchester for his PhD in 2018, and at the time of recording in 2022 he held an EPSRC postdoctoral fellowship there. He was first author of the 2020 Nature Communications paper on Brown-Zak fermions in graphene superlattices.

item.description:
Jessica Henty-Ridilla studies the cytoskeleton, which she describes as the bones of your cell. In her lab that means two proteins, actin and microtubules, which are constantly built up and taken apart, like Lego. She wants to know how the two coordinate, and what happens when that regulation goes wrong in diseases such as ALS.

About the guest

Jessica Henty-Ridilla was an assistant professor at SUNY Upstate Medical University in Syracuse, New York, when we recorded this episode in 2022. Her faculty profile now lists her as an associate professor in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, and in 2024 her lab received a $2.2 million grant renewal to continue its protein research. Her lab combines cell biology, genetics, advanced microscopy and test-tube reconstitution of the cytoskeleton.

Since 2021 he has held the Chair of Pharmaceutical Biology at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU). He holds an ERC Starting Grant (2020), and his research looks for new biogenic routes against infectious and inflammatory diseases and characterises new natural products.

Gregor Fuhrmann curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from April 5 to April 11 2020. Read all of Gregor’s tweets from that week.

About the guest

Thomas Swift is a Lecturer in Polymer Chemistry at the University of Bradford, UK, studying functional polymers, both biological and synthetic, for uses from removing substances from solutions to diagnostics, adhesives and property modifiers. A highlight is a bacterial sensor published in 2019. Thomas worked in R&D for a paint manufacturer before an industrially sponsored PhD in Sheffield.

Thomas Swift curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from March 22 to March 28 2020. Read all of Thomas’s tweets from that week.

Tanvir Hussain was an Associate Professor at the University of Nottingham when we recorded this episode. He is now an EPSRC Research Fellow and Professor of Coatings and Surface Engineering in the Faculty of Engineering at the University of Nottingham.

Tanvir Hussain curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from March 8 to March 14 2020. Read all of Tanvir’s tweets from that week.

Frankenstein on the Nanoscale
Frankenstein on the Nanoscale with Amy Gelmi
item.description:
About the guest

Amy Gelmi was a Vice Chancellor’s Research Fellow at RMIT University when we recorded this episode. She is now a Senior Lecturer in the School of Science at RMIT University, working in biomaterials, tissue engineering and nanoscale characterisation.

Amy Gelmi curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from February 29 to March 7 2020. Read all of Amy’s tweets from that week.

item.title: From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach
From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach
From Shampoo to LCD – a Theoretical Approach with Charlie Wand
item.description:
About the guest

Charlie Wand is a Postdoctoral Researcher at The University of Manchester, UK, a computational chemist working on soft matter, from liquid crystals in phone displays to surfactants in shampoo, simulating molecules as virtual beads. Work at the University of Cambridge developed a computational approach to calculate the solubility of large molecules. Charlie did a chemistry degree and a PhD at the University of York.

item.title: Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale
Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale
Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale with Izzy Jayasinghe
item.description:
About the guest

Izzy Jayasinghe was a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow and Lecturer at the University of Leeds when we recorded this episode. She is now an Associate Professor at UNSW Sydney, recruited in 2023 as Head of the Department of Molecular Medicine in the School of Biomedical Sciences. Her Signalling Nanodomains Laboratory combines the super-resolution microscopy tools it develops with existing technologies to study how cell signals trigger a heartbeat and drive other bodily functions.

item.title: Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry
Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry
Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry ft. Laia Castilla-Amorós
item.description:
About the guest

Laia Castilla-Amorós is a Doctoral Assistant in the Lab of Nanochemistry of Energy at EPFL, Switzerland, developing the synthesis of multimetallic colloidal nanoparticles. Colloidal chemistry has so far reached only trimetallic nanoparticles, which usually contain at least one noble metal; her work pushes towards copper-based, noble-metal-free multimetallic nanoparticles as catalysts for electrochemical CO2 reduction, starting with CuGa nanodimers.

Laia Castilla-Amorós curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from February 2 to February 8 2020. Read all of Laia’s tweets from that week.

item.title: Building New Medicines
Building New Medicines
Building New Medicines with Kameron Kilchrist
item.description:
About the guest

Kameron Kilchrist is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at Janssen Research & Development, USA, a biomedical engineer designing better drug delivery technologies using science at every scale, from proteins to whole organisms. A recent highlight is a new assay that measures endosomal disruption in live cells, a key step in how nanoparticle drug carriers deliver their payload. The path ran through a tissue engineering lab and computational image analysis.

DNA Origami: Building Synthetic Cells with Kerstin Göpfrich
item.description:
About the guest

Kerstin Göpfrich was a Max Planck Research Group Leader in Heidelberg when we recorded this episode. She is now a professor at the Center for Molecular Biology of Heidelberg University (ZMBH). Göpfrich’s ERC project ENSYNC uses DNA and RNA origami to build a prototype synthetic cell that can evolve.

Kerstin Göpfrich curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from January 12 to January 18 2020. Read all of Kerstin’s tweets from that week.

Queer and Quantum Magnetism
Queer and Quantum Magnetism with Andrew Princep
item.description:
About the guest

Andrew Princep is the Keeley-Rutherford Junior Research Fellow at Oxford University and STFC, UK, using neutron and X-ray beams to study how atoms are arranged and interact in materials. He published the most complete measurements of the magnetic properties of yttrium iron garnet, a material behind an emerging technology for transmitting information. He studied nanotechnology before a master’s in neutron scattering and a PhD in X-ray measurements of rare-earth intermetallics.

item.title: Tiny Magnets - What are they for?
Tiny Magnets - What are they for?
Tiny Magnets - What are they for? ft. Tim Dreier
item.description:
About the guest

Tim Dreier is a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies, Sandia National Laboratory, USA, making tiny magnets to study how they behave and how they can be used. Earlier work covered polymers containing tiny gold particles and how gold forms ultra-small clusters in solution, including a study of the claimed catalyst Au25(SR)18. He started graduate school as an organic chemist and was a postdoc at Los Alamos.

Tons of Nanomaterials: Big Science and Little Details
Tons of Nanomaterials: Big Science and Little Details ft. Matthew Jewell
item.description:
About the guest

Matthew Jewell was an Associate Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Eau Claire when we recorded this episode. He is now Chair of the Materials Science and Biomedical Engineering Department there. His group studies the mechanical properties of superconducting materials for large magnets: YBCO tapes and Bi-2212 and Nb3Sn round wires.

Matthew Jewell curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from December 9 to December 14 2019. Read all of Matthew’s tweets from that week.

item.title: Little Lights with Big Ideas
Little Lights with Big Ideas
Little Lights with Big Ideas ft. Rachel Oliver
item.description:
About the guest

Rachel Oliver is a Professor in the Department of Materials Science & Metallurgy at the University of Cambridge and Director of the Cambridge Centre for Gallium Nitride. Her group studies nanoscale structures in gallium nitride to improve electronic and optoelectronic devices, including porous GaN. She is Chief Scientific Officer of the spinout company Poro Technologies.

Rachel Oliver curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from December 2 to December 7 2019. Read all of Rachel’s tweets from that week.

item.title: Squeezing Light with Nano Antenna
Squeezing Light with Nano Antenna
Squeezing Light with Nano antenna ft. Thorsten Feichtner
item.description:
About the guest

Thorsten Feichtner is the Managing Director of the Cluster of Excellence ct.qmat at the University of Würzburg, Germany. His research improves light–matter interaction with optical antennas, metallic nanoparticles designed to route photons into tiny volumes, and he developed a method that uses evolutionary optimisation to design them. He did his diploma and doctorate in Würzburg, in the group of Bert Hecht.

item.title: Graphene Smoothie
Graphene Smoothie
Graphene Smoothie ft. Matthew Diasio
item.description:
About the guest

Matthew Diasio is a PhD Candidate at the University of Virginia, USA, making graphene by mixing graphite at high speed in liquids and studying how the liquid’s properties affect the amount and quality of graphene produced. The work showed that thicker, syrup-like liquids make more graphene by applying more stress. An interest in astronomy turned to materials research after a chemistry seminar, lab work and two internships on carbon nanotubes.

Catching Light at Ten to the 9th
Catching Light at Ten to the 9th ft. Poornima Peiris
item.description:
About the guest

Poornima Peiris is a Student and Researcher at Harvard University, USA, working with a nanophotonics group on the absorption of nanomaterials, multispectral analysis, and nanostructured semiconductors and metallic nanowires, used to make electromechanical and photonic sensors for precision medicine, agriculture and environmental monitoring.

Poornima Peiris curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from November 11 to November 16 2019. Read all of Poornima’s tweets from that week.

Playing Snooker with Atoms ft. Clara M. Barker

About the guest

Clara M. Barker is the Lab Manager for the CfAS Materials department at Oxford University and Dean of Equality and Diversity at Linacre College, UK. A thin film materials scientist, she makes films often less than a micrometre thick for superconductors, solar cells, solid-state batteries and optical coatings, and once coated spinal implants to improve their biocompatibility. She trained in electronic and electrical engineering and worked in industry before moving into materials research.

Steve Maguire is a Staff Scientist at SNOLAB in Canada and runs Science Isn’t Scary. During his MSc at the University of Ottawa, he found a quick, simple way to make silver nanoparticles with UV light, producing a better product than earlier photosynthesis methods; his former group built a research area on those first experiments.

Steve Maguire curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from October 28 to November 2 2019. Read all of Steve’s tweets from that week.

item.description:
About the guest

Upulie Divisekera is a Researcher at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, and Co-founder of Real Scientists. The doctoral work looked for new ways to deliver drugs to specific cells using tiny gold carriers. Earlier work in cancer immunology included an anti-CD73 immunotherapy that shrank tumours in mice and is now in clinical trials.

Upulie Divisekera curated the Real Scientists Nano Twitter account (@RealSci_Nano) from May 17 to May 23 2020. Read all of Upulie’s tweets from that week.

Olga Shimoni is an Associate Professor and PI at the University of Technology Sydney, Australia, studying how nanotechnology can improve medical devices, especially for detecting disease early. The project closest to a commercial product is an easy, non-invasive screening test for celiac disease developed by her team.

Svenja Lohmann is a PhD Candidate in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Uppsala University, Sweden, using ion beams from particle accelerators to analyse materials. Drew Evans was an Associate Research Professor at the University of South Australia when we recorded this episode. He is now Professor and Dean of Research in the College of Engineering and IT at Adelaide University, having moved with UniSA to the new Adelaide University in 2025. His research group in the Future Industries Institute works on the performance and manufacturability of materials for industry, including commercialising conducting polymers for energy storage.

item.title: Dancing Light at Nanoscale with Siva Shakthi
item.description:
About the guest

Siva Shakthi is a PhD student in Physics at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Thiruvananthapuram, India, working in microwave photonics using nonlinear optical processes in single-mode optical fibres. The work includes notch filters and optical switches for optical communication, and the observation of a tunable Fano effect in Brillouin scattering spectra. Siva holds a Bachelor’s in Physics and an MSc in Physics specialising in laser science.
